name: Cessna 172 Skyhawk
description: The four-seat, high-wing Cessna 172 Skyhawk is, in its maker's words, the most popular single-engine aircraft ever built. In 2025 it celebrated 70 years in the air, and it's where countless aviation stories begin.

name: Piper J-3 Cub
description: Light, slow and covered in fabric, the Piper J-3 Cub shows the four forces at their gentlest. First built in 1937, it sold for $1,300, and 19,888 Cubs had been built when production ended in 1947, many in Piper's bright yellow.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Piper J-3 Cub

name: de Havilland Canada DHC-2 Beaver
description: De Havilland Canada surveyed bush pilots before designing the rugged, all-metal Beaver, which first flew on August 16, 1947, and could fly from short strips on wheels, floats or skis. Its maker's own pages differ on how many were built: about 1,600 or 1,692.

sources.title: DHC-2 Beaver in Canada Post's Canadians in Flight series

name: Extra 300
description: First flown on May 6, 1988, the Extra 300 was the first two-seat Extra, with a carbon-fiber wing spar and skin. Aerobatic planes like it fly upside down at air shows by setting the wing at the right angle of attack.

name: Pitts Special
description: Curtis Pitts built the first S-1 in 1945, and his small, agile biplanes went on to dominate unlimited aerobatic competition in the 1960s and 1970s. In aerobatics, a spin is a stall on purpose. The oldest surviving Pitts is at the Smithsonian.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Pitts S-1C Special

name: Junkers F 13
description: In June 1919, the Junkers F 13 became the world's first passenger airplane made of metal, with a cabin for four passengers. More than 300 were built, and they were part of Lufthansa's first fleet when the airline was founded in 1926.

sources.title: NACA Aircraft Circular No. 6: All-Metal Junkers Airplane, Type F 13

name: Boeing 727
description: Designed for smaller airports with shorter runways, the Boeing 727 was the first Boeing jetliner with triple-slotted flaps. It first flew on February 9, 1963, became the first commercial airplane to pass 1,000 sales, and 1,832 were built.

name: Lockheed Constellation
description: With its curving fuselage and three tail fins, the Lockheed Constellation is easy to spot. It introduced hydraulically boosted flight controls, and in April 1944 one set a transcontinental speed record, flying nonstop from Burbank to Washington, D.C., at an average 331 mph.

sources.title: How the Constellation Became the Star of the Skies

name: de Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter
description: First flown on May 20, 1965, the Twin Otter was designed for the harsh conditions of Canada's far north. It can operate on wheels, skis or floats and is known for short takeoffs and landings, serving operators in over 100 countries.

name: Beechcraft Bonanza
description: The Beechcraft Bonanza first flew in 1947 with a distinctive V-tail, and it's still built today. Its maker calls it the longest continuously produced aircraft in history. More than 18,000 have been delivered, and today's model uses a 300-horsepower piston engine.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Beechcraft 35 Bonanza

name: Lockheed F-104 Starfighter
description: Nicknamed “the missile with a man in it,” the F-104 Starfighter was built around a 14,800-pound-thrust J79 turbojet with an afterburner. It was the first US interceptor able to fly at sustained speeds above Mach 2.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Lockheed F-104A Starfighter

name: Boeing 777
description: The Boeing 777 was the first jetliner designed 100 percent digitally, preassembled as a 3D computer model instead of a full-scale mock-up. It first flew on June 12, 1994, with a choice of turbofans from three engine makers.

name: Lockheed C-130 Hercules
description: The prototype YC-130 first flew on August 23, 1954, lifting off after a ground roll of just 855 feet. Powered by four turboprops and built with high wings for rough airfields, the Hercules has had the longest continuous production run of any military aircraft.

name: Consolidated NY-2 Husky
description: On September 24, 1929, Jimmy Doolittle flew a Consolidated NY-2 Husky from takeoff to landing by instruments alone, the first flight of its kind, with a hood hiding the view outside. Its new artificial horizon, directional gyro and sensitive altimeter soon became standard.

sources.title: Flying Blind: Doolittle's first instrument flight

name: Boeing 767
description: The widebody Boeing 767 first flew on September 26, 1981, with a two-pilot computerized flight deck shared with the 757. In 1985 it led the way for extended-range twin-engine flying, becoming the first commercial twinjet on regular routes across the Atlantic.

name: Airbus A320
description: First flown on February 22, 1987, the Airbus A320 was the first civil aircraft with full digital fly-by-wire, flown with sidesticks instead of yokes. Its family has drawn more than 20,100 orders, and Airbus calls it the most successful in commercial aviation history.

name: Boeing VC-25A
description: Two modified 747-200Bs, the VC-25As, replaced the presidential 707s in 1990, and either becomes Air Force One when the president is aboard. Each has 4,000 square feet of floor space, with an office, living quarters and galleys that can serve 100 people at a sitting.

name: Airbus BelugaXL
description: Based on the A330, the Airbus BelugaXL carries wings, fuselage sections and other large parts between Airbus sites. It can fly two 30-meter wings at once. Six are in service, each painted with a smiling face chosen by Airbus employees.

name: BAe 146
description: Its maker highlights the four-engined BAe 146's exceptional slow-speed handling and steep approach capability. In 1986, two BAe 146s joined The Queen's Flight to carry Britain's royal family, and the type has since been converted into aerial firefighters too.

name: Boeing 757
description: The Boeing 757 first flew on February 19, 1982, and 1,050 were built over a 23-year run. FAA wake turbulence rules name it specifically: controllers typically keep small aircraft 4 miles behind a 757.

name: Airbus A321XLR
description: The Airbus A321XLR is the longest-range Airbus single-aisle airliner, able to fly up to 4,700 nautical miles and stay aloft for up to 11 hours. Airbus pitches it for routes such as New York to Rome and London to Vancouver.

name: Douglas World Cruiser
description: In 1924, four Douglas World Cruisers left Seattle to fly around the world with no radio and few navigation aids beyond an earth inductor compass. After 175 days and about 27,550 miles, two of the original four completed the first flight around the globe.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: The Story of the First Flight Around the World

name: Boeing 787 Dreamliner
description: First flown on December 15, 2009, the Boeing 787 Dreamliner uses carbon-fiber composites for up to half of its main structure. That lets its cabin sit at 6,000 feet, 2,000 feet lower than conventional jets, behind the largest windows on any widebody flying today.

name: Lockheed WP-3D Orion
description: NOAA's two WP-3D Orions, nicknamed Kermit and Miss Piggy, fly into hurricanes on purpose. On missions of 8 to 10 hours they cross the eyewall into the calm eye, dropping instrument probes that radio back pressure, humidity, temperature and wind.

sources.publisher: NOAA Office of Marine and Aviation Operations
sources.title: Lockheed WP-3D Orion

sources.publisher: NOAA Office of Marine and Aviation Operations
sources.title: NOAA Hurricane Hunters

name: Montgolfier Balloon
description: On November 21, 1783, a Montgolfier hot air balloon carried Pilâtre de Rozier and the marquis d'Arlandes on the first free flight by people. The brothers who built it came from a French family that had made paper for generations.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Montgolfier Balloon

name: 1903 Wright Flyer
description: At Kitty Hawk on December 17, 1903, the Wright Flyer made the world's first successful flights of a powered, heavier-than-air flying machine. Its 12-horsepower engine drove two propellers that the brothers designed as rotating wings.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: 1903 Wright Flyer

name: Blériot XI
description: A Blériot Type XI monoplane carried Louis Blériot from near Calais to Dover on July 25, 1909, the first airplane flight across the English Channel. Three years later, Harriet Quimby flew a Blériot monoplane the other way.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Blériot XI

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Blériot's Cross-Channel Flight

name: Ryan NYP Spirit of St. Louis
description: Built by Ryan for Charles Lindbergh, the Spirit of St. Louis carried its fuel tanks ahead of the cockpit, so he looked forward through a periscope. On May 20–21, 1927, it made the first solo, nonstop flight across the Atlantic.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Ryan NYP Spirit of St. Louis

name: Sopwith F.1 Camel
description: Named for the hump over its two guns, the Sopwith Camel entered service in July 1917. Its powerful rotary engine made it tricky to fly but very agile, and Camels downed 1,294 enemy aircraft, more than any other Allied fighter.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Sopwith F.1 Camel

name: Douglas DC-3
description: First delivered to American Airlines in June 1936, the DC-3 carried 21 passengers by day, while its sleeper version bedded 14 overnight. Airlines bought 455, the military another 10,174 as C-47s, and hundreds were still flying decades later.

name: Boeing 314 Clipper
description: Boeing built just 12 Model 314 Clippers between 1938 and 1941. These flying boats used the wings of the giant XB-15 bomber, and in 1943 President Franklin D. Roosevelt flew in one to meet Winston Churchill at Casablanca.

name: Supermarine Spitfire
description: The prototype Spitfire, K5054, first flew on March 5, 1936, with test pilot Joseph “Mutt” Summers at the controls. Designed by Reginald Mitchell around a thin elliptical wing and a Rolls-Royce Merlin engine, more than 20,000 were eventually built.

sources.title: The first flight of the Spitfire

name: North American P-51 Mustang
description: The P-51 Mustang was the first single-engine fighter based in Britain to reach Berlin. More than 14,000 were built, and 8,302 of them were D models, with a bubble canopy and six machine guns.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: North American P-51D Mustang

name: Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress
description: The B-17 was the first Boeing military airplane with an enclosed flight deck instead of an open cockpit. Counting the 5,745 built by Douglas and Lockheed's Vega, 12,726 Flying Fortresses were made, yet only a few survive today.

name: Vought F4U Corsair
description: The Vought F4U Corsair first flew on May 29, 1940. Its bent gull wings gave its big propeller extra ground clearance, and it stayed in production longer than any other US fighter that served in World War II, reaching 12,582 built.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Vought F4U-1D Corsair

name: Messerschmitt Me 262
description: The Messerschmitt Me 262 was the world’s first operational jet fighter, with two turbojets and sleek swept wings. Its factories built 1,443, but only about 300 saw combat before the war ended.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Messerschmitt Me 262 A-1a Schwalbe (Swallow)

name: Bell X-1
description: Shaped like a .50-caliber bullet and dropped from a B-29, the rocket-powered Bell X-1 became the first airplane to fly faster than sound on October 14, 1947. Chuck Yeager named it Glamorous Glennis after his wife.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Bell X-1 Glamorous Glennis

name: de Havilland Comet
description: The de Havilland Comet first flew on July 27, 1949, and entered service on May 2, 1952, as the world’s first jet airliner. It was also the first airliner with a highly pressurized cabin and fully hydraulic flight controls.

sources.title: Comet: The World's First Jet Airliner

name: Boeing 707
description: The Boeing 707's 100-foot cabin was the largest passenger cabin in the air, and its extra wing sweep let it fly about 20 mph faster than the rival Douglas DC-8. Its left-side front and rear doors became standard on later Boeing jets.

name: Boeing 747
description: The Boeing 747 jumbo first flew on February 9, 1969. NASA later turned two 747-100s into carriers for the Space Shuttle, and two 747-200Bs became the presidential VC-25As.

name: Airbus A300
description: Airbus’s first airliner, the A300, flew on October 28, 1972, as the world’s first twin-engine widebody. Airbus Industrie had been formed in 1970 to build it, and 821 A300-family aircraft were eventually produced.

sources.title: 50th anniversary of the A300's first flight

name: Boeing 737
description: The first 737 was the last new airplane built at Boeing's Plant 2, whose building was too low for its tail, so a crane attached the tail in the parking lot. Lufthansa took the first production 737 on December 27, 1967.

name: Airbus A380
description: The largest passenger plane ever built, the A380 has a full-length double deck and wings spanning 79.8 meters. Its fleet of 251 aircraft has carried more than 300 million passengers since entering service in 2007.

name: Concorde
description: Concorde first flew on March 2, 1969, and began passenger service in January 1976, carrying up to 100 people at twice the speed of sound. Twenty were built in all, and every one was retired by 2003.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Concorde, Fox Alpha, Air France

name: Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird
description: Built largely of titanium by Lockheed's Skunk Works, the SR-71 Blackbird cruised above Mach 3 at about 85,000 feet with a crew of two. Its engines stayed in afterburner for the whole cruise.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird

name: North American X-15
description: The rocket-powered X-15 still holds the world speed record for a winged, powered aircraft: 4,520 mph, Mach 6.7, set in 1967. Eight of its pilots flew above 50 miles and were recognized as astronauts.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: The X-15 Still Holds The World Speed Record 50+ Years Later
X-15 Space Pioneers Now Honored as Astronauts

name: Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor
description: The F-22 Raptor became operational in 2005. It can supercruise, flying faster than Mach 1.5 without afterburners, and Lockheed Martin says its 195 jets were the world's only operational fifth-generation fighter fleet when the last was delivered in 2012.

name: Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk
description: First flown on June 18, 1981, the angular F-117 Nighthawk was the world's first operational stealth aircraft. It entered service in 1983, but the US Air Force kept it secret until 1988. Lockheed built 59.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: F-117 Nighthawk Joins the National Air and Space Museum Collection

name: Boeing CH-47 Chinook
description: The tandem-rotor Boeing CH-47 Chinook entered US Army service in 1962. Its two rotors turn in opposite directions, so it needs no tail rotor. Boeing has said upgraded Chinooks will stay in the Army's fleet through at least the 2030s.

name: Antonov An-225 Mriya
description: With a maximum takeoff weight of 640 tonnes, the six-engine An-225 Mriya was the world's heaviest aircraft. Built to carry the Buran space shuttle on its back, it first flew in 1988. The only one completed was destroyed in 2022, in the war in Ukraine.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.title: The Strength and Resolve of Ukraine

name: NASA's Boeing 720 Crash-Test Jet
description: In 1984, NASA and the FAA flew this four-engine Boeing 720 by remote control into a planned crash, to learn how to make accidents more survivable. Crash-test dummies rode in its seats, and 97% of its sensors were working at impact.

sources.title: Flight Test Experience and Controlled Impact of a Remotely Piloted Jet Transport Aircraft

name: Airbus A350
description: Every modern airliner, including the Airbus A350, is built under rules shaped by past accidents, from fire-resistant cabins to tougher fatigue standards. The A350's airframe is 53% composites and 14% titanium, which Airbus says cuts weight and maintenance.

name: Airbus A330
description: The twin-engine Airbus A330 regularly flies long routes over oceans. In 2009, Europe's aviation safety agency cleared it for ETOPS (extended operations) beyond 180 minutes, letting its routes stray up to 1,700 nautical miles, a little over four hours, from a suitable airport.

name: Gulfstream G650
description: The Gulfstream G650 can fly at up to Mach 0.925, close to the speed of sound. One set a record for large-cabin jets that aren't supersonic, flying westbound around the world in 41 hours and 7 minutes.

name: Joby S4
description: The Joby S4, listed by the FAA as the Model JAS4-1, carries a pilot and four passengers on six tilting electric propellers at up to 200 mph. Joby says it makes 45 decibels in cruise, heard from 500 meters (1,640 feet) away.

sources.title: Airworthiness Criteria: Joby Aero Model JAS4-1 Powered-Lift

name: Boom XB-1
description: On January 28, 2025, Boom's XB-1 flew at Mach 1.122 near Mojave, California, which Boom says made it the first independently developed jet to break the sound barrier. Instead of Concorde's drooping nose, it showed its pilot the runway through augmented reality.
